ch-e1b.subject: Chemistry
ch-e1b.question:
hey, I do Chemistry SL and ESS SL (exams May 2027). In ESS my teacher said the ocean is 'about 30% more acidic' than before the Industrial Revolution because surface ocean pH has dropped from about 8.2 to 8.1. how can 0.1 be 30%?? so I need help with both:
CHEM PART:
(a) Calculate [H+] in seawater at pH 8.2 and at pH 8.1. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in [H+]. Is 'about 30%' right? [2]
(c) Write equations to show how CO2 dissolving in seawater increases [H+]. [2]
(d) Explain why the concentration of carbonate ions (CO3^2-) goes down as the ocean becomes more acidic. [2]
(e) Some models predict a surface pH of 7.8 by 2100. By what factor would [H+] be higher than at pH 8.2? [1]
Please make the numbers really clear because I need them for the ESS part.
ch-e1b.response_text:
(a) [H⁺] = 10^(−pH) mol dm⁻³
At pH 8.2: [H⁺] = 10^(−8.2) = 6.31 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³ [1]
At pH 8.1: [H⁺] = 10^(−8.1) = 7.94 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³ [1]

(b) Ratio: [H⁺] at pH 8.1 ÷ [H⁺] at pH 8.2 = 7.943 × 10⁻⁹ ÷ 6.310 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.259 (this is 10^0.1) [1]
Percentage increase = (1.259 − 1) × 100 = 25.9%, so about 26% [1]
So "about 30%" is not right; it overstates the change. The pH scale is logarithmic, so a fall of 0.1 pH unit multiplies [H⁺] by 1.26 wherever the pH starts. A 30% rise would need a pH fall of about 0.11 units. If your teacher's source says 30%, check the exact pH values it uses.

(c) CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq)
CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) [1]
H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq) [1]
Overall: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq)

(d) The extra H⁺ is taken up by carbonate ions, which act as Brønsted–Lowry bases: CO₃²⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) [1]
Raising [H⁺] shifts this equilibrium to the right (Le Chatelier's principle), so more CO₃²⁻ is converted to HCO₃⁻ and [CO₃²⁻] falls [1]

(e) [H⁺] at pH 7.8 = 10^(−7.8) = 1.58 × 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³
Factor = 1.58 × 10⁻⁸ ÷ 6.31 × 10⁻⁹ = 2.5 (10^(8.2 − 7.8) = 10^0.4 = 2.51) [1]

Numbers for the ESS part:
- [H⁺] at pH 8.2 = 6.31 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³
- [H⁺] at pH 8.1 = 7.94 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³
- Rise in [H⁺] from pH 8.2 to pH 8.1 = 25.9% (about 26%), not 30%
- [H⁺] at pH 7.8 = about 2.5 times the value at pH 8.2

If your teacher's source gives more precise pH values, send them and I will recheck part (b).

maa-e1a.subject: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
maa-e1a.question:
Hi, I take Maths AA SL and History HL, both exams May 2027. In History we're doing Paper 2 authoritarian states (Hitler) and I want to use the 1923 hyperinflation in my essay, and in maths we've just done exponential models so I thought I could use that lol. I've pasted the bread prices table from my History textbook below.
MATHS PART (Paper 2 style, GDC allowed): Let t be the number of months after January 1923 and P the price of a loaf of bread in marks. Use the model P = P₀e^(kt) with the January 1923 and November 1923 prices from the table.
(a) Write down P₀ and find the exact value of k, then give k to 3 sf. [4]
(b) Find the factor that prices were multiplied by each month according to the model. [2]
(c) Find how many days it took prices to double according to the model (take 1 month = 30 days). [3]
(d) Use the model to predict the price in July 1923 and compare it with the actual July price in the table. Comment on whether the model is a good fit for 1923. [3]
Please show the log working. The history bit needs these numbers so make them clear.

supplied_texts.title: Price of a loaf of bread in Berlin, 1918–1923 (table from the student's History textbook, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Table typed in by the student
supplied_texts.text:
Price of a loaf of bread in Berlin, 1918–1923

Date | Price of a loaf of bread (marks)
December 1918 | 0.63
December 1922 | 163
January 1923 | 250
July 1923 | 3,465
September 1923 | 1,512,000
November 1923 | 201,000,000,000

maa-e1a.response_text:
Assumed: Maths AA SL (you said SL); Paper 2 style, so a GDC may be used for decimals; t = 0 is January 1923, so November 1923 is t = 10 and July 1923 is t = 6; prices are in marks.

(a) P₀ = 250, the price at t = 0.  A1
At t = 10: 2.01 × 10¹¹ = 250e^(10k)  M1
e^(10k) = 2.01 × 10¹¹ / 250 = 8.04 × 10⁸
Taking natural logs: 10k = ln(8.04 × 10⁸)  M1
ln(8.04 × 10⁸) = ln 8.04 + 8 ln 10 = 2.084429… + 18.420681… = 20.505110…
Exact: k = (1/10) ln(8.04 × 10⁸), which is 2.050511…
k = 2.05 (3 s.f.)  A1

(b) P(t + 1) = P₀e^(k(t + 1)) = eᵏ × P₀e^(kt) = eᵏ × P(t)  M1
Exact factor: eᵏ = (8.04 × 10⁸)^(1/10)
eᵏ = e^(2.050511…) = 7.77187…
Each month the model multiplies the price by 7.77 (3 s.f.)  A1

(c) Doubling means 500 = 250e^(kt), so e^(kt) = 2  M1
kt = ln 2, so t = ln 2 / k = 0.693147… / 2.050511… = 0.338036… months  M1
Days = 30 × 0.338036… = 10.14…, so the price doubles in 10.1 days (3 s.f.)  A1
Exact: 300 ln 2 / ln(8.04 × 10⁸) days.

(d) July 1923 is t = 6.
P(6) = 250e^(6k) = 250e^(12.303066…)  M1
= 5.509 × 10⁷, so 5.51 × 10⁷ marks (3 s.f.)  A1
The table gives 3465 marks for July 1923. The model is about 1.59 × 10⁴ times the table value (5.509 × 10⁷ / 3465 ≈ 15 900).
Comment: the model is not a good fit for 1923.  R1
It is built from the January and November prices only, so it matches those two points by construction and says nothing about the months between. The table's growth is not constant: from January to July the price multiplied by (3465/250)^(1/6) ≈ 1.55 per month; from July to September by (1 512 000/3465)^(1/2) ≈ 20.9 per month; from September to November by (2.01 × 10¹¹ / 1 512 000)^(1/2) ≈ 365 per month. The single factor 7.77 is close to none of these three rates.

Key numbers for the History paragraph (model results unless stated):
January 1923 price (table): 250 marks
k = 2.05 per month, exact (1/10) ln(8.04 × 10⁸)
Monthly factor: 7.77
Doubling time: 10.1 days
July 1923: model 5.51 × 10⁷ marks; table 3465 marks
Use the unrounded k: with k = 2.05 the July prediction is 5.49 × 10⁷.
These numbers describe the table and the model only; they do not show why prices rose.

Marks shown are a provisional allocation.

Next step: in the History paragraph, set 5.51 × 10⁷ (model) beside 3465 (table) and say the model uses only the January and November prices.

mai-e1.subject: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
mai-e1.question:
Maths AI SL, exams May 2027. Two questions from my paper 2 revision pack (GDC allowed):
1. Priya buys a car and borrows €18 000. The loan is repaid in equal monthly instalments over 5 years, at an annual interest rate of 6.5% compounded monthly.
(a) Calculate her monthly payment. [3]
(b) Calculate the total amount she pays back. [2]
(c) Calculate the total interest she pays. [1]
(d) Find the amount she still owes after 2 years. [3]
2. The heights of sunflowers in a field are normally distributed with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 12 cm.
(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen sunflower is taller than 190 cm. [2]
(b) 10% of the sunflowers are shorter than h cm. Find h. [2]
(c) 400 of the sunflowers are measured. Find the expected number that are taller than 190 cm. [1]
can you show what I'm supposed to put into the GDC as well? our teacher says we lose marks if we don't write the TVM inputs. answers to 3 sf, money to 2 dp
mai-e1.response_text:
Question 1 [9 marks]

Sign convention for the finance solver: money received (PV) is positive; money paid out (PMT) is negative; a balance still owed (FV) comes out negative. Payments are made at the end of each month, with P/Y = C/Y = 12.

(a) Let $M$ be the monthly payment in euros.

$$18\,000 = M \times \frac{1-\left(1+\frac{0.065}{12}\right)^{-60}}{\frac{0.065}{12}}$$

Finance solver: $N = 60$, $I\% = 6.5$, $PV = 18\,000$, $PMT = ?$, $FV = 0$, $P/Y = 12$, $C/Y = 12$, giving $PMT = -352.1907\ldots$ (M1A1)

Her monthly payment is €352.19. (A1)

(b) Total repaid $= 60 \times 352.19$ (M1)

$= 21\,131.40$

She repays €21 131.40 in total. (A1)

The total uses the payment actually made, €352.19 to the cent.

(c) Total interest $=$ total repaid $-$ amount borrowed $= 21\,131.40 - 18\,000 = 3131.40$ (A1)

She pays €3131.40 in interest.

(d) The amount owed after 2 years is the balance after the 24th payment, so $N = 24$.

Finance solver: $N = 24$, $I\% = 6.5$, $PV = 18\,000$, $PMT = -352.19$, $FV = ?$, $P/Y = 12$, $C/Y = 12$, giving $FV = -11\,491.11$ (M1A1)

Check by a second route: $\left(1+\frac{0.065}{12}\right)^{24} = 1.138429\ldots$, so $18\,000 \times 1.138429\ldots - 352.19 \times \dfrac{1.138429\ldots - 1}{\frac{0.065}{12}} = 20\,491.72 - 9000.61 = 11\,491.11$

After 2 years she still owes €11 491.11. (A1)

Using the unrounded payment, €352.1907\ldots, the balance is €11 491.10; the answer above uses the payment actually made.

Question 2 [5 marks]

Let $X$ be the height of a sunflower in cm, with $X \sim N(170,\, 12^2)$. The GDC normal inputs take the standard deviation, $\sigma = 12$, not the variance.

(a) $P(X > 190)$ (M1)

Normal probability, lower bound 190, upper bound a very large number, $\mu = 170$, $\sigma = 12$: $P(X > 190) = 0.04779\ldots$

So $P(X > 190) = 0.0478$ (3 s.f.). (A1)

(b) $P(X < h) = 0.10$, so $\dfrac{h - 170}{12} = -1.28155\ldots$ (M1)

Inverse normal, area to the left 0.10, $\mu = 170$, $\sigma = 12$: $h = 154.621\ldots$

So $h = 155$ cm (3 s.f.). (A1)

(c) Expected number $= 400 \times P(X > 190) = 400 \times 0.04779\ldots = 19.116\ldots$

The expected number of sunflowers taller than 190 cm is 19.1 (3 s.f.). (A1)

Mark annotations show a likely allocation and are provisional.

hi-e1a.subject: History
hi-e1a.question:
Hi, I take Maths AA SL and History HL, both exams May 2027. In History we're doing Paper 2 authoritarian states (Hitler) and I want to use the 1923 hyperinflation in my essay, and in maths we've just done exponential models so I thought I could use that lol. I've pasted the bread prices table from my History textbook below.
HISTORY PART: My essay question is 'To what extent was the economic crisis of 1923 the main reason why Hitler came to power in 1933?' My claim is that hyperinflation was the main reason people started voting for the Nazis. Write me ONE body paragraph (max 300 words) that tests my claim, using the maths results and dates. If my claim is wrong please tell me!
(Hand-off from the router: the Mathematics specialist's answer to the maths part of this request has been relayed to you through the hub as the document peer:maa-e1a. Where you use its results, quote them exactly and attribute them to the Mathematics specialist.)

supplied_texts.title: Price of a loaf of bread in Berlin, 1918–1923 (table from the student's History textbook, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Table typed in by the student
supplied_texts.text:
Price of a loaf of bread in Berlin, 1918–1923

Date | Price of a loaf of bread (marks)
December 1918 | 0.63
December 1922 | 163
January 1923 | 250
July 1923 | 3,465
September 1923 | 1,512,000
November 1923 | 201,000,000,000

hi-e1a.response_text:
Hyperinflation was not the main reason people began voting for the Nazis, because the dates separate the two. The textbook table shows prices rising fastest in the autumn of 1923, from 1,512,000 marks in September to 201,000,000,000 in November, and the Mathematics specialist's rates show the acceleration: "≈ 1.55 per month" from January to July, "≈ 20.9 per month" from July to September and "≈ 365 per month" from September to November. Yet a currency reform in November 1923 stopped the inflation, and the Nazi party, banned after Hitler's failed Munich Putsch that same month, was still small at the 1928 Reichstag election. The model cannot bridge that gap. The Mathematics specialist states that "the model is not a good fit for 1923", because "It is built from the January and November prices only, so it matches those two points by construction and says nothing about the months between." Its July 1923 prediction of "5.51 × 10⁷ marks" is "about 1.59 × 10⁴ times the table value" of 3,465 marks, so it cannot show what prices did, and, in the specialist's words, "they do not show why prices rose." The electoral surge came in the 1930 Reichstag election, nearly seven years after the inflation peaked, once the Depression had reached Germany from 1929. The dates therefore point to the Depression as the economic crisis that matters for the Nazi vote. The 1923 collapse may have left voters with a lasting fear of inflation that the Nazis later used, but the table cannot test that, and a source on voters' attitudes would be needed. The claim, as worded, fails.

Limit: the Mathematics report's own checks flag its written lines "ln 8.04 + 8 ln 10 = 2.084429" and "ln 2 / k = 0.693147" as not holding as written. The rates and the July figure above agree with the table, but do not copy those two lines into the maths answer.

Next step: build the thesis on the Depression and treat 1923 only as a qualified aside.
